Federal Business Development Bank

subsubtopic: RENUMBERING OF CERTAIN SECTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the hon. Minister of State for Small Businesses and Industry (Mr. Huntington) on bringing this bill back. I, too, had made representations to the government House leader asking him to bring it back because the Federal Business Development Bank is critically important to small business in this country. Unless this bill were passed, as the minister has said, it would have meant a reduction in the number of loans that the FBDB was able to give from a rate of 1,500 a month to a rate of approximately 500 a month, and great many small businesses would have suffered as a result.
These are difficult times for small businesses because of the high interest rates, high fuel prices and so on. It is no time for us to be letting down small business by failing to pass a bill such as this one. On listening to the minister's remarks this evening, I should like to congratulate him on his strong support for the Federal Business Development Bank. It has been an extremely successful institution. It has helped many thousands of small businesses. It has a very fine track record, in spite of the fact that it is not a highly profitable Crown corporation. It does not intend to be a highly profitable Crown corporation. Merely it intends to be roughly a "break even" Crown corporation performing a service for small businessmen in Canada.
There has been a very dramatic increase in some of the aspects of the Federal Business Development Bank in the last couple of years. They have a program called the "Counselling Assistance to Small Enterprise", which is commonly known as CASE. For example, the number of businesses counselled in just the last two years has risen from 1,660 in 1977 to 5,400 in
1978,	to 9,700 in the current year. That is a very dramatic growth in a very important service which helps educate small business people on how to run their businesses better. It encourages more small business people to start up in business, to expand their business, and prevents a lot of unnecessary bankruptcies due to lack of knowledge.
There has been a dramatic increase in the number of jobs provided as a result of the FBDB. They break them down into three categories: those jobs started, which in just two years have risen from 3,000 to 18,000; jobs increased, which in three years have risen from 2,500 to 14,400; and jobs maintained, which they show as rising from 690 to about 4,000. This is very commendable work by the Federal Business Development Bank. We want to see that kind of thing continued.
The great majority of small businesses in Canada are Canadian-owned. They pay taxes, they provide jobs, and they provide management know-how in future expansion. We wish to see them continue to have the services of the Federal Business Development Bank. We wish to see that done as promptly as possible.
If I may, I should like to say to the minister that in his first comments on this act, when he introduced it on October 24,
1979,	he referred to the advantage of changing the ratio, as we are doing in this bill, so as to allow more loans to be made by the Federal Business Development Bank. He said the following:

The advantage that this would have is that no additional federal budgetary expenditure for paid-in capital would be required.
He indicated that no such additional expenditure would be required and instead they could use more leverage, as it is known in the financial community. This is absolutely true and we hope that it will carry us through the balance of the fiscal year. I would urge the minister, in looking ahead, to use his influence on the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) in the coming budget to provide additional paid-in equity capital, because the future work of the Federal Business Development Bank will depend on additional budgetary outlays. To cut back on these sorts of budgetary outlays indeed would be a very false economy when we want to see the country growing, new jobs provided, and particularly to encourage small and medium-size Canadian-owned businesses.
Also in committee the minister said that he favoured continual growth in the loans of the FBDB, and we applaud that. He said that he favoured a continued growth in the CASE program, and we applaud that too. As I have said, we urge the minister to use his influence. Certainly we will back him up to the extent we can. We urge him to use his influence with the Minister of Finance in the coming budget to make sure that the Federal Business Development Bank is financed properly for both the CASE program and an adequate equity base, so that the loan program can continue as well.
These are tough times for small businesses. We want to see small business getting every break it can. One of its best friends is the Federal Business Development Bank. We urge the passage of this bill as promptly as possible and future budgetary increases for this valuable institution for small business in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find it very interesting that the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Phillips) kept his comments so brief. When I outline some of the increases in interest rates which have been effected through the Federal Business Development Bank, perhaps we might have some idea why his remarks were kept rather brief in relation to the small business community.
If we look to January 1, 1978, we find the FBDB charging roughly 9.5 per cent on loans at that time which were running around $50,000. If one calculates it out, one can see that the average per annum cost on that would be around $4,750. Under the previous administration we saw a number of rather rapid increases in the interest rate. On January 4, 1979, roughly a year later, it went up to $6,625, an increase from 9.5 per cent to 13.25 per cent. I am sure a lot of small businessmen took a look at that increase in interest costs and noted that it was a $1,875 increase in that one 12-month period.
As we know, there was a change of administration in May of this year, and by this fall-as a matter of fact today-we see that the interest rate is around 16 per cent. The costs in terms of interest rates alone on a $50,000 loan now would be about $8,000. That is an increase from January, 1978, of $4,750, to about $8,000 now. The increase from January of this year to now was roughly $1,400. That is an increase of a

considerable amount, if one looks at a small businessman and knows that that probably is not the only loan he carries.
One thing which 1 think is important in looking at a riding such as Skeena is that there were roughly 350 customers serviced by the Terrace branch of the FBDB. Their loans averaged almost exactly $50,000. Roughly $17.5 million is out at this time. If we look at the increases from January, 1978, to January, 1979, their increase in interest rates was $650,000. It is important to look at the bill itself. I notice the hon. member for Vancouver Centre has left already, but the hon. minister is still here. One of the interesting things 1 noticed, when doing some background work before speaking tonight, was a question put to the minister as reported in last month's issue of the Financial Times. The questioner asked:
I gather that the government is considering turning the Federal Business Development Bank over to the private sector. What is your position on this?
I have run down part way in the article there, and I find the minister saying this:
If the Federal Business Development Bank was privatized it would lose some of the services it's performing to the marginal borrowing needs of the business community. If you privatized it, there would have to be a form of guarantee available to any private bottom-line operator in that area.
I am glad to note that the minister went on to say:
1 don't find a lot of complaints from the banking community on FBDB activities.
However, the questioner goes on to ask:
Why is it being considered for privatization?
The minister goes on to say:
I think everything should be considered on a sunset basis-entitled to review to find out how well that agency or that corporation is serving the objectives which caused it to be formed and put in place in the first place.
This is a question the minister will have to address himself to: exactly what is going to happen to the function of the FBDB? The same amount of capital is still in there that the government has put in, but we have seen a very dramatic request for an increase in the amount to be loaned out from ten to 12, with the possibility of it increasing to about 15.
We should look carefully at the small business community in this country. This is a vital sector of the economy. About one-third of Canadians are employed there directly, and 90 per

cent of these small companies employ fewer than 200 people. The major difference between small businesses and large corporations in this country is that the small businesses, be it one or two employees, or up to 200, must respond very, very quickly to any market changes within our economy. They are extremely labour intensive, particularly as compared to large resource companies. I think there is a point to be made there when we look at the broad scale of taxation legislation, and the types of tax shelters and everything else that exist for the large resource companies which have a tendency to be much greater machinery oriented as compared to the labour intensity of the small companies.
If we look, for example, at the mining sector, which gets a 100 per cent write-off of costs, and compare that to small businesses, which run generally in the one-third taxation ratio, we see that small business does not have the same sort of opportunity to get large quantities of new machinery, even such items as a Xerox machine, in order to develop and get into the market.
If we look at bankruptcies which have taken place in the last number of years, particularly under the previous administration, we see that the greatest level of bankruptcy is among small businesses, and I suggest among the very small businesses and those that have been in operation less than six years.
Big businesses such as oil companies have been systematically eliminating small businesses. A classic example of this has been in relation to the small independent service stations and regional suppliers of energy within this country. We have seen the very large oil companies, Exxon, Imperial, Gulf, Texaco, all of them, moving very quickly to get their hands on the small gas stations.
I think we all remember not too many years ago when the gas pumps were only part of what we expected at a gas station. There was always a good mechanic on hand, and it was one of the most vigorous and competitive parts of our small business sector because there was an attempt always to have someone who was good at a number of things available on-site, as well as to pump gas. We have seen almost the complete elimination of that by the large petroleum corporations. I think that is a very sad thing, and something to which the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Industry (Mr. Huntington) has not addressed himself, to this point in this House.
The needs of small business in this country are really two. The first is money, and the second is information. As we know, and I am sure the minister knows, cash flow, particularly during the start-up period, is one of the most crucial matters from small businesses.
If we look at one of the reasons for capital intensive corporations getting the sort of tax breaks they get, we will see that the economy of this country has typically been one of advantage to them. I know speakers on that side of the House and also to my right have frequently suggested that we are hewers of wood and drawers of water. I think this is becoming even more true under the present regimes we have seen, particularly in relation to high interest rates.

Mr. Speaker, the chartered banks increased loans under $1 million by over $2 billion, ten times the activity of the FBDB.
Three times since coming to office the Conservatives have increased interest rates. The banks' prime rate for their best customers is now at 14 per cent, with the rate for small business even higher. Only one chartered bank, the Bank of British Columbia, has a preferential small business rate half a point below the prime.
Why should there be a high interest rate policy? I suggest it is because the Bank of Canada, supported by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie), believes that excess private spending and public spending are causing inflation. In fact, as a number of economists have pointed out, it is supply problems which are causing inflation, particularly increases in the cost of food and energy. As we saw last month with the release of the September CPI figures, which recorded an increase in the inflation rate from 8.4 per cent to 9.6 per cent, it was oil, electricity, beef, dairy products, and coffee that were the main contributors to inflation.
The high interest rate policy will make it more difficult for small business to expand. For those who can afford to take out a loan, it will increase the cost of doing business. The FBDB pointed out in its annual report that many of its customers are exporters. The increased cost of producing goods for export will make our goods less competitive. The latest trade figures for August recorded a deficit of $141 million in merchandise trade, our first monthly deficit in over a year.
With high interest rates, we may see more monthly trade deficits this year. Prior to the release of the August trade figures, the Minister of Finance was predicting that our international balance of payments deficit on goods and services would total $7 billion. This is a substantial increase from last year's $4.3 billion deficit. With a continuing tight money policy, this deficit may go even higher.
The effect of high interest rates also shows up in bankruptcies. The latest Figures show a total of 1,762 bankruptcies in September, which is up 8.6 per cent from September, 1978.

Sorry, Mr. Speaker. The Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) and the Minister of Finance have indicated that they will not make good on their election promise of a $2 billion tax cut for Canadians. Such a move will have an adverse effect on small businesses, many of which are retailers. Statistics Canada has reported that for two years in a row, 1977 and 1978, family income in this country has fallen behind increases in inflation. Looking at statistics for this year, we see that weekly wages are continuing to decline in real terms. The effect of this erosion of income has been a decline in consumer
November 26, 1979

spending, particularly for durables such as appliances, furniture, etc. Even spending on non-durables like food is stagnating. More money is being saved, which is a prudent move for families who may be facing unemployment as a result of the government's restrictive policies.
A third policy of the federal government which will have a greater impact on small business than this increase in FBDB lending is its energy policy. It has been estimated that a $1 a barrel increase in oil prices will lead to a loss of 20,000 jobs. The Conservatives are talking of a $4 a barrel increase. Where will those 80,000 jobs be lost? While it is impossible to be precise, we can assume that energy-intensive industries will be hardest hit by the price increase. Down the line, their suppliers, including small manufacturers, will lose contracts and jobs.
The government has said that inflation is the number one problem to be overcome. Through the Bank of Canada it has said that it must increase interest rates in order to avoid the inflationary impact of a further fall in the dollar. Certainly the cost of imports increases when the dollar falls, and this causes inflation to increase. But there are other ways to combat the effects of a falling dollar than to keep raising interest rates. The government could embark on a program of import substitution. It could encourage Canadians to buy goods manufactured in this country. It could assist manufacturers, especially small businesses, struggling to compete against low cost imports. Certainly we cannot turn around Canadian buying patterns overnight, but we have to start sometime.
If the government continues its shortsighted policy of raising interest rates time and time again, we will not only lose jobs in the short run, but we will make ourselves more dependent on foreign capital to bail us out of our balance of payments difficulties. This, in turn, will tie us more closely to international interest rate trends, whether or not they are harmful to Canadian businesses. If the government wants to do something for small business in this country, it should first abandon its current interest rate policy.
I trust that the minister will turn his mind to dealing with the high interest rate problem, hopefully through the Bank Act, to encouraging his cabinet colleagues to do something in that order and, in fact, to dealing with the FBDB by other means such as, for example, in terms of collateral or in terms of dealing directly with the interest rates at their source.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the present debate on the Federal Business Development Bank.
I am in a position to appreciate the job done by this bank since it was originally established to help small and medium-size businesses, and particularly those located in remote areas such as the one I represent, namely, the lower St. Lawrence, the Gaspe peninsula, the North Shore of the St. Lawrence and the maritimes. Many businessmen never would have prospered and developed that region were it not for the help granted by
Federal Business Development Bank
the Federal Business Development Bank. All in all the bank accomplished its task well. It is normal and logical that the provision of the act which created it be revised to allow it to continue its work and offer the same services to small business in our country.
Mr. Speaker, we support this bill because it has always been our view that the banking system should serve the people and not the other way around. The Federal Business Development Bank came into being because chartered banks refused to take their responsibilities and extend loans to small and medium-size business. Chartered banks serve big business with our money and have never been concerned with their responsibilities towards the economy in general and small business in particular. Last year, some of them increased their profits by 35 per cent over previous years.
I recall quite well having asked, a number of times, the former minister of finance in the previous government to have an inquiry made into this. The report of the bank superintendent had then been submitted to the finance minister and stated there was no abnormal situation. It certainly was not abnormal for the chartered banks which were raking in huge profits, but it was certainly totally unacceptable for those of us who have to struggle in a world that is ever more uncertain. And small enterprises are not excluded from this situation. They are the ones which are most likely to meet with difficulties in unfavourable economic circumstances since bank credit is less easily accessible to them.
That is why I welcome this new legislation which will enable the FBDB to raise the amount and the number of loans it grants to businesses. Moreover, it will probably continue to help a number of small enterprises get started and set up shop in the economic world. Our less developed regions are relying heavily on this bank for their development. As I said earlier, the chartered banks are not those which have helped us or will help us in the future.

On the recommendation of the Minister of Finance, the governor in council may, by order, increase the factor referred to in subsection (1) by which the aggregate of the direct and contingent liabilities of the corporation referred to in that subsection may exceed the capital of the corporation to a factor not exceeding fifteen.

Mr. Speaker, I want to join with my colleague, the hon. member from Vancouver, in congratulating the bank for the liberal philosophy it seems to be pursuing. On the other hand, I sympathize a lot with the minister who is working to improve small and medium-size businesses while his colleague, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Lawrence), tries to destroy certain small businesses. The bottlers are an example, Mr. Speaker. It is inconceivable that while the minister wants to develop small and medium-size businesses, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs should do everything to break up a sector of our economy which is very important and on which a great many people rely to earn a living.
Small and medium-size businesses, Mr. Speaker, benefit from the FBDB, and 1 think we should go a lot further. I think that bank should also become an instrument of regional economic expansion. Several sectors, several ridings in Canada cannot benefit from the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and must rather turn to the FBDB. It is unfortunate that the bank management should be somewhat congested and that some of our small entrepreneurs should not have the chance to avail themselves entirely of its services.
In this difficult year, Mr. Speaker, where the government has decided to raise interest rates, I think all small entrepreneurs, and certainly those in my riding, in Argenteuil, are having enormous difficulties surviving. It is very important that the minister take that into consideration and that he use his power to expand the bank's capacities to help the small entrepreneurs in Argenteuil. The small entrepreneur, Mr. Speaker, has no chance against the heavy bureaucracy and all that paperwork he must fill out to get information.
So I repeat for the information of the minister it would seem if we could bring about a stronger regionalization of the FDBD, the services the bank can make available to small entrepreneurs would be more justified. Often in Quebec we see businesses get off the ground, stay in business for a while, and then disappear. Why? In Quebec we had the recreational vehicles, like skidoos and other pleasure vehicles-we had several in the Drummondville area-and it is sad to see, Mr. Speaker, that 90 per cent of those industries have now closed their doors or have been sold to U.S. multinationals. The only one we have left which is a tribute to the country is Bombardier which also had, of course, to branch off into other fields to be able to survive.
Mr. Speaker, this was a case where ingenious people decided to create jobs and businesses and were unable to remain solvent because of a lack of capital. In my opinion, this is where the Federal Business Development Bank could play a role. It is very important for Canada to have some type of risk

capital to help the founders of industries create new businesses, especially in the secondary and tertiary sectors. We know that the primary sector has no problem in developing. Why should some group in the Federal Business Development Bank not get involved especially with industry, tourist services and hotel services, of course?
I am convinced that if the bank took this type of action, we could create many jobs in this difficult period brought about by our friends opposite. With interest rates at the present level, I believe it is important for the minister to think seriously about instructing the bank to open up its purse and provide a greater chance for small Quebec entrepreneurs, especially those in my constituency of Argenteuil who, as you know, Mr. Speaker, have great difficulty in creating job opportunities.
Unemployment has reached 33 per cent in certain areas of my constituency. The few cents that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Alexander) was good enough to grant us through the Canada Works program will not be enough to help a constituency with so much unemployment, but if we could have an even more liberal policy through the Federal Business Development Bank, as I said earlier, we could really create permanent jobs.
This is why I urge the minister to consider these sectors. Since the constituency of Argenteuil is not an area designated by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, we must find another formula to help small and medium-size businesses of the area.
I have already spoken about a new system, perhaps for Mirabel, and about tax-free zones. Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that this would be in the same context. If a tax-free zone were created around Mirabel, and through the policies of the Federal Business Development Bank, I am convinced that we would launch new businesses and at the same time create jobs.
In concluding I would say that I agree with the amendments to this legislation. I wanted to stress those points and I hope the minister has taken notice of the few suggestions I have made, particularly on the problem of bottlers in Canada. They are all small or medium-size businesses that his colleague, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs appears bent on destroying, which would hurt consumers who would have to pay higher prices for those products. It seems to be the policy of our Tory friends to do such things.
I do sympathize with the minister because I know his duty is not easy, but I am convinced that with his good will he will find ways to help small and medium-size businesses and to enable the Federal Business Development Bank to play a greater role in that field about which we are so much concerned.

Mr. Speaker, my intervention in this debate will be very brief. The measure before us is a small step in the right direction. However, as with the mortgage tax credit scheme, it does not compensate for the large difficulties faced by small business people.
I come from an immigrant family. For a number of years my parents operated a small business. I was involved in small business as well. While it is very gratifying to be a small businessman, there are major problems a small businessman faces, especially in the economic milieu. We exist in an economic system with great fluctuations of booms and busts. Every time there is a boom it is like the mushroom season. Many small businesses crop up. People invest their life savings in a small enterprise. Then by forces totally beyond their control, the season is over, and thousands of these small businesses are wiped out. Everything the family worked for and invested in is wiped off the map. No wonder we have one of the highest business failures in this country. I understand it is roughly 8 per cent.
Having a viable sector of the economy controlled and operated by small business people is essential to the well-being of this country. It is able to supply services that larger businesses and government operations often are not able to supply. It has a flexibility and a sensitivity to the needs of the particular community and neighbourhood.
In order to make a viable small business environment we, as a country, first have to stabilize our economy. We need economic planning. There must be economic certainty so that when an individual invests in a small business venture, often his life savings, he can be guaranteed that the need for that service will be there ten, 20 years down the road.
What we now see is the opposite. Large chains and multinational corporations which can withstand losses come into a community and wipe out the small entrepreneur. That has been done in many areas; food, housing construction, and retail outlets. Those are but examples. There used to be many small businesses in Regina. A number of these have disappeared over the years.
What about service stations?

My colleague mentions service stations. They have changed drastically in the last decade. Many neighbourhood grocery stores have been wiped out. We used to have different contractors building homes. Many of these have become sub-contractors, if they were lucky. Most homes are now built by large development corporations.
There may be some argument in terms of scale and efficiency, but that is a very small and narrow argument. When you take the larger perspective of the community good and social good, very often the larger corporations and chains contribute very little to the local community. They use the local community as a way of sucking out money and resources, and very often put very little back.

I suggest also that in the dealings the federal government has with small entrepreneurs, the bureaucracy and the complexity of the many forms the entrepreneurs have to fill out, are obvious stumbling blocks. The Income Tax Act requires a lawyer to take advantage of all the loopholes and all the corners in that particular act, and only large corporations with corporate lawyers are able to take advantage fully of the act. Most small business people are not able to take advantage of all the sections of that act. In addition, I urge another step that the federal government could take in encouraging small business people, and that is that the Department of Supply and Services accept as a policy that it will buy its needed goods and services from small operators, small business people and people from local communities, rather than taking a very narrow point of view in terms of what is economic. I suggest that, when the government defines what is economic, it use a larger measuring stick and determine what is economic and good for the community as a whole. I think if the government, in view of the amount of buying the government does, would use that economic power it has to help small business operators in this country, it would do much to strengthen that sector of the economy.
Contrary to what members of the two old-line parties repeatedly say, members of the New Democratic Party are not opposed to the small businessman. In fact in many ways we are indeed the champions of the small businessman. We realize that when working people have decent wages, it is the small business people who benefit. We realize that when farmers have a decent return on their investment and their labour, it is the small business people who benefit. We realize that when income falls back and does not keep up with the cost of living, it is the small business people who get mowed down first. In order to have a strong economy we need a strong small business sector. We need decent incomes, decent wages, and a decent return to farmers.
We will never get it with a high interest rate.
Of course, as my hon. colleague has mentioned, all these things are not possible with a program of high interest rates.
Just spend more.

An hon. member suggests we should spend more. Of course it is spending which allows the small business person in this economy to keep going. If we are to follow the advice of the hon. member opposite, it will be the small business people who will go down because they cannot afford to borrow the money to keep themselves afloat until the next boom in our industrial period. The system of booms and busts is the basic enemy of small business people because they do not have the power and the ability to see themselves through the

bust period into the next boom period. Ultimately it is economic planning and controlling economic forces which will benefit small business people and give them the stability they need to thrive and grow in our economy.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say a word or two in connection with small business, mostly because throughout my constituency as I knock on doors and visit, people are very concerned about a number of things regarding small business.
This government is creating a climate in which people will be happy to invest their money. One of the things during the last few years was that it became very, very difficult for anyone to invest money in Canada, to the extent that many people decided to invest their money in other countries. We have become so bound up with regulations, red tape, and environmental concerns that many times small businesses get so frustrated that they just simply give up. I think one of the things we are going to have to do, if we are going to get small business to the point where it can do the job it can do in this country, is to cut some of the red tape and unshackle free enterprise so that it can have a chance to work.
I have known people who have submitted plans to planning boards for subdivisions two, three, and four times. They simply get them sent back without even any suggestion as to what is wrong with them. People become fed up when it takes two years to get a plan approved. That is too much red tape and too much regulation.
People do require money. I was very happy the other day to hear that the Alberta Opportunity Company is stabilizing its interest rate at 12 per cent and that, in smaller centres, they will go even below that. In larger cities they may go slightly above that, but that gives the businessman some stabilization factors. He knows that he is not suddenly going to be hounded by an increase because the rate in the country increases, and then finds that instead of the rate that he signed for he is going to have to pay two, three, four or five cents more on the dollar, which is enough to ruin many businesses.
I think we should endeavour to encourage our banks to stabilize bank rates and not put in contracts which, if the rate increases, then they will change the contracts. This is ruining some businesses in this country today. One motel operator told me that if there is one more increase in interest, he is ruined. He just cannot stand it.
Tell that to your finance minister.

It is due to the fact that he took his loan out at a rate of 11 per cent, and then it goes up and up every time there is an increase in the country. This is not fair to the person who takes out a loan, and I just question this banking practice.
Another thing which irritates me and many, many other people is that the International Development Bank or other banking institutions provide money only on a first refusal basis. I realize that we do not want to put commercial banks out of business, but when we do it on a first refusal basis, it

leads to all types of conniving. Banks themselves write notes of refusal simply to help the entrepreneur get a loan. But when a person makes an application and if a bank says, "Yes, we will give you the money", at some exorbitant interest rate such as 15 per cent or 18 per cent and refuses to write a first refusal, then of course the man is left in a terrible position because he does not have the refusal and therefore government banks will not even consider his application. I think there has to be something done so that if we are going to insist on a first refusal, that first refusal has to be based on a reasonable rate of interest or, if we refuse to give a refusal but say, "We will lend the money at an exorbitant rate of interest", a rate that a business could never repay, then it should be considered a first refusal.
One of the other things mentioned by an hon. member a moment or so ago is the paper work which people object to greatly, but one of the major items which has discouraged initiative in this country has been the capital gains tax. This was brought in by the former administration, and it is killing initiative throughout this country.
What are you doing about it?

When people pay their income tax on what they earn year after year, and when they finally get to the place where they want to sell their businesses, the government should not be taking another bite out of it so they do not have enough left to live on during their retirement the way they had planned.
I met a man on a street of one of the towns in my riding. He pointed to the store that he owned where he employed seven people, and he told me he also owned the lot next to that store. He said, "If there were no capital gains tax, I would expand my business and hire another five or six people. The opportunity is here and I would like to do it, but I will not build up a tremendous estate for the government to chop up when 1 want to sell the business. If they take away the capital gains tax, I will work 18 hours a day to build up an estate for my children and my children's children, but I am not prepared to do it for any government." This tax has killed initiative in this country, the initiative in all businesses, including farming. It is hurting this country and keeping investment down.
I do not know how many other hundreds of people are not expanding because they have arrived at the stage where they do not want to expand. They can sell the business but they are afraid of the big chunk, of the lump, that will be taken out in the capital gains tax, and that they will not have enough on which to live. So the capital gains tax is an excellent means of killing initiative among our entrepreneurs, farmers, and other businessmen.

Federal Business Development Bank

speakerposition: Minister of State for Small Businesses and Industry
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, and I thank hon. members for many of their comments tonight. My life has been an energetic one, full of hard work. I have come through the depression and I know the value of a job. I have never wanted to be without one, and I have tried to pass that desire on to my progeny. So I become very troubled when I hear people with the apperance and bearing of the hon. member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong) who lash out at large corporations and say that these large chains suck the life-blood out of communities. He startles me with that kind of lack of understanding of the present age, of the present society, with his lack of understanding of the very components of a free enterprise society.
I should like to point out to the hon. member that the large chains in this country and many of the largest businesses, from the biggest steel companies to the large grocery chain stores, provide the most opportunities and create the base for small and medium-size enterprises. It is these large corporations that create the most jobs, and it is their efficiency in the distribution and movement of goods to consumers that creates opportunities. Business after business has started, has innovated, and has supplied the exciting, vibrant type of marketplace. To say that these large organizations suck out the life-blood of communities is a statement that I never thought I would hear in this chamber.
Where have you been all this time?

speakerposition: Minister of State for Small Businesses and Industry
speechtext:
I should like to pay tribute to the hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Deniger) who spoke earlier, who had a career in the Federal Business Development Bank, and who knows full well the qualities, the leadership, and the management skills that the incumbent president brought to that organization, the president who has built the FBDB up to be a frontier of service for the entrepreneur who is starting out, or for the one who has started out and has a cash flow need or a working capital need which is beyond the normal restrictions of chartered banks.
We have also heard tonight from a few members who want the bank to loosen up its pocket book and to let money out without proper analysis and examination. I do not agree with such a stance because the bank, particularly since it is a Crown corporation, has a responsibility to the borrower. It spends a great deal of its resources in its CASE organization, where they have retired businessmen who act as counsellors at a very low fee and who use their experience to give assistance, aid, and advice to allow an enterprise to have an opportunity to survive. A banker who lends money carelessly to a borrower is not doing that borrower a service, because there is tragedy in borrowing money and not sustaining sufficient cash flow to pay it back. That is something that no person wants to carry the rest of his life, because it takes energy out of the individual and sets him aside for almost a decade while he is recovering. I do not think a good banker wants to see that happen.
Staying power seems to be the greatest need in the Canadian business community today. What do we mean by staying power? It does not mean spending wildly, nor does it mean
1718

November 26, 1979
Federal Business Development Bank
borrowing recklessly. It means managing and conserving a cash flow resource. It means saving. It does not mean buying a big car or spending needlessly. It means protecting the working capital, it means putting some strength aside in the bank for unforeseen events, because the world of business is a very exciting world for those who have the right mentality and the courage to stay in that world. You are dealing with all of the disciplines. You are dealing with computers, engineers, accountants, and lawyers. You have all these disciplines serving the person who has developed the skill or the staying power in the business community.
1 myself come from the small business community, and I have built four or five businesses. But those businesses have survived alongside very large businesses. I learned many years ago that if I was going to survive, I would not try to do business with the giants but rather would try to match my own size and my own abilities. However, it is the large chains and department stores that offer opportunities of doing things better. What I would like to say to hon. members here tonight, particularly to those who sit with the hon. member for Regina East, is that there are tremendous opportunities in finding something that is sloppy or soft out there in our community. Any time you find something that is not being done effectively or where there is some room for productivity, hard work, a good mind, the ability to work, some dollars and the courage to borrow properly, there is an opportunity there. Let me tell you that to have created one of those opportunities, to have given it staying power, to have created jobs, is a pretty comfortable thing to carry forward through life, and I commend it to anybody with the strength to do it.
There is another aspect to the job in which I find myself, having come from that small business sector and having had a great and exciting life in it. When the former leader of the opposition in the last parliament appointed a small business critic, I wondered what it was all about. I was told that that is politics and, being a businessman, I am not credited with having too much political savvy. However, since I have been in this job I have wanted to point out how good the small business community was.
Under the previous government, the small business secretariat consisted of a team of six persons with a staff of eight, who played an advocacy role within the government and dealt with different departments of government on behalf of the small business community. They had a definition of the small business: in the manufacturing sector, 100 employees or less, and in the service sector, 50 employees or less. Then I had to scratch my head and say, "Well, here we have a department which is playing an advocacy role, and we have the Federal Business Development Bank playing a front line role in a very high calibre way, providing much social purpose to its thrust and the part it plays in the business community". But we started to find a very interesting picture in the small and medium enterprise sector in Canada.

We looked down at the United States with its small business act. They built a massive bureaucracy to feed the small business world. They have a full-time committee, the Congress, the Senate, a big bureaucracy, and definitions for small business in each of 52 sectors. They have put in regulation and legislation on top of legislation. There are probably more people working in the bureaucracy than in the small business community, for all I know. I did not want to go that route. I have rationalized the route that perhaps we should be looking at here.
I looked at a survey done by the small business secretariat on the tax returns of 1976. This was all done in a very confidential manner, but the figures which came out of it were not part of the added paper burden in another Statistics Canada study. The figures in 1976 showed that there were 1,075,000 businesses in Canada. Of those businesses, 325,000 were incorporated. That leaves unincorporated some 750,000 businesses, 429,000 of which were involved in the selfemployed professional salesmen, farmer, and fishermen categories.
It is interesting that 99 per cent of the total number of businesses in Canada had annual sales of less than $2 million. The total sales for all of those businesses in 1976 were $392.2 billion. The incorporated businesses did some $347.6 billion of that, leaving $44.6 billion for the unincorporated businesses. Those figures in themselves show some of the power which is in that community.
Another interesting statistic which came out of this study was that in 1976 total employment by business in Canada was 6.6 million people. Businesses which had sales of less than $2 million per year employed 2.5 million people. If one added the finance sector into that figure, with $2 million and less in sales a year, there were 2.8 million people employed, or 42 per cent of all business employment was in the small business category doing $2 million or less in sales per year. If one moves up into the medium sector category of $20 million or less in sales, there were 4.1 million people employed in that sector, or 66 per cent of the total employment in Canada. That shows why in Canada, France, Germany, and the United States so much emphasis is put on the small and medium sector by governments.
Over a year ago the President of France announced a whole policy for the small business sector in France. I think that is some of the awareness I would like to create as I come out of the early gestation period of this ministry in which I find myself. We should know that 25 per cent of the total sales from businesses in Canada originate with businesses doing less than $2 million a year in Canada, and that 52 per cent of the total sales done in Canada originate in the medium and small sector doing less than $20 million in sales a year.
Another interesting figure is that the business contribution to the gross national product in Canada is 42 per cent, and 30 per cent of the business contribution to the gross national product originates from firms doing less than $2 million in annual sales a year. Also 55 per cent of the business gross
November 26, 1979

national product originates from firms doing less than $20 million in annual sales a year. I am very pleased tonight to have a few minutes of the time of the House to put this perspective on the record and in place for members, to illustrate the growing importance which this part of Canadian life has, this part of life which any industrial nation has.
We have heard quite a few comments tonight about high interest rates. Nobody, believe me, nobody likes high interest rates. 1 lived through a monetary crisis back in 1956 and very nearly lost a business. There was another crisis which I and others survived in 1972, but some fell. At that time they restricted the ratio of lendings to deposits. In other words, they retrenched or restricted the supply of money. They did not increase the cost of money. They just dried up and tightened up the supply. 1 have asked bankers, "Why did you not go that route again?" The gentleman who is the president of the Federal Business Development Bank explained in some detail the problem of going that retrenchment route.
One thing we must do today is create good jobs and provide good work. When one restricts the supply of money to businesses which have a legitimate expansion going in the marketplace, one restricts the creation of legitimate work and growth. The bankers told me that that is what they did not want to repeat, and that is why they tried another route.
It does not matter what we do or what we put in place in the way of law, minds will find little angles in the wording to find a way around it. In this particular case the monetary community down in Washington, rather than restrict supply and dampen down legitimate growth in the global and domestic marketplace, decided to increase the cost of money. When they increased the cost of money, they started to put pressure on all the loose leverage, loose fringe borrowing and stock market activities going on which created and added to inflation. When they increased the cost of money, all of that had to fall out and start to wring out.
I said to an executive vice-president of a bank whom I met at a reception here in town about one or two weeks ago, "Did you really have to increase the cost of money the way you did? How serious is the drain of dollars out of the country?" He said, "Ron, if we did not match the short-term interest rates, we have in short-term deposits maturing in our bank alone today $340 million". That is one day, one bank. If that money cannot be held at home, what is the other alternative? One can retrench supply and dampen down everything, all the good creation in legitimate business.
The other alternative to high interest rates is to keep interest rates down and watch the dollar fall. We found out that we could sell more goods in the global marketplace by allowing our dollar to slip from $1.03 to 95 cents and all the way down to 85 cents. We saw hundreds of millions of dollars, even billions, being poured out into reserves to stabilize it at that place. Then those manufacturers and resource companies which could sell in the marketplace all of a sudden came up to capacity and started delivering their goods out to the world.
Federal Business Development Bank They tell me now that there is no more manufacturing capacity which can take advantage of a dollar lower in value than 85 cents, and therein lies the dilemma in which we find ourselves.
The president of the Federal Business Development Bank reports to me at least once a week. He is a most attentive person and wants his minister to be as informed as he can be on a subject as complicated as this. He and I have talked this over, rationalized it, and have asked: Can I increase the rate of the bank? As I have said several times in the House, loans of $50,000 are at 16 per cent and loans over $50,000 are at 16.5 per cent. The small business person is getting a break from the bank.
We have a bill here tonight, C-4, whereby we are widening from one to ten the ratio of lending to one to 12, the difference the bank has to go to the marketplace for, and in going from one to ten to one to 15 before we get the new act through we are increasing the cost of money to that bank, this Crown corporation, by three tenths of one per cent on what we are doing tonight.
If we change the agency status and do a few other things to the bank, each one of those moves will increase the burden of cost on that bank. At the moment the bank's cost of service is 4.25 per cent over the cost of money. I just cannot agree or go along with the hon. member for Argenteuil (Mr. Gourd) when he suggests that we loosen up, give cheaper rates and everything else. That bank is on a teeter-totter performing tremendous social services.
We have talked about category three and four loans. Those are loans that get into trouble and you need a postponement, interest has to be postponed, principal has to be postponed, or both, and then you have to put them to rest. As the hon. member for Laprairie suggests, give them a little patience, a little staying power, and sometimes you will get winners from that little group and they will go on, having learned their lesson.

Do you think you will make it until ten
o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Small Businesses and Industry
speechtext: 1 am going to do my best. Applaud me if I do.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of State for Small Businesses and Industry
speechtext:
1 am just trying to keep it interesting for you. 1 want to return to the hon. member for Regina East who was lashing and thrashing out against the large corporations and chains. I forgot about him over there for a minute or two. As I have walked through life I have seen a lot of altruism in people in the business world. They work hard. Sure, they sharp pencil and they must have some self-interest or they cannot survive. There are great sectors of our community that attack the old self-interest motive. Believe me, the self-interest motive builds things, creates things, and does create jobs.
As I have gone down through the years, coming upon one Red Cross drive after another, one big community effort after another, and as I have watched the Kiwanis Club and the

November 26, 1979
Federal Business Development Bank
Rotary Club making their efforts, and have come across campaigns for the crippled children's hospitals, I have wondered where all that effort has come from. Who supports all that effort? I have seen presidents of the large chains and corporations give half a year just to the chairing of one of these altruistic activities in the community. I really do get disturbed when that part of altruism, and that part of being part of the community are not given true justice or respect just because an individual comes out of the business community. Not all people can stand the rugged nature of the small and medium-size enterprise sector. Some would rather be working for the government or for large corporations because it is more exciting and more stable. As 1 said in Quebec City at a seminar the Federal Business Development Bank had on down there-
MacMillan Bloedel has had four presidents during the last half dozen years.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Small Businesses and Industry
speechtext: What does that have to do with it? Look at all the jobs that MacMillan Bloedel provides. Look at all the pension schemes, the machinery, the development, the infrastructure, and look at the new pulp mill that is going up at Powell River; look at all of this growth and I will tell you something. The small and medium-size enterprise sector cannot provide the benefit package that large corporations can provide. There is a great mix out there. I guess one of the challenges 1 have is to get that small and medium-size enterprise sector of this country up to a standard of health whereby their benefit package can match that of government employees or that of the employees of MacMillan Bloedel. 1 have watched MacMillan Bloedel and other large corporations put on funding drives that made possible Simon Fraser University. Can you imagine that?
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of State for Small Businesses and Industry
speechtext: Can you imagine that hotbed of socialism out there on the west coast up on that beautiful mountain which was made possible by the executives of large corporations in western Canada? It was very tolerant about what happened to it, and it is a very pleasant surprise to see Simon Fraser University maturing at long last. My God, what a youth it has had; what a binge! My good friend behind me says it has had a change of management and there has been a big improvement.
Thirteen minutes to go.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Small Businesses and Industry
speechtext:
Stanley, I wish I had your staying power. While I am gathering my thoughts for the next 13 minutes, I would just like to say this. We have some great challenges ahead of us in this country. This free enterprise system can survive. A consciousness has to exist in the business community. I think I have seen in the last decade a great awareness on the part of people in that community for what we now call good corporate citizenship.
Since I have been in office for the past six months I have seen presidents of large corporations come in and very careful-

ly explain how their procurement policies and everything else assist the small and medium-size enterprise sector. We have come a long way down the road toward stabilizing a lot of the injustices and irrational decisions which have been hard on people. We are not going to get rid of it all.
Let me say this, sir. In the small business community there are behavioral problems. This is also the community that fights hard, is used to competition, and is used to eating a lot of beans. I do not know of too many people in that sector who can survive and get staying power unless they are very careful with their savings. They cannot spend all they make.
There are some major questions today that will have to be addressed. The questions which face us in respect of the economy in the 1980s include the following: will Canada be able to maintain the productivity level and the productivity growth necessary to maintain competitiveness with other countries? That is an essential thing, and it is one of the great challenges we are facing over in the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce today.
We have in place protective mechanisms that are protecting industries which cannot compete globally. I think those industries have an obligation behind that curtain to bring themselves up to the optimum level of productivity. We need the difference in that resource in other areas whereby we can lift emerging industries up to global competing standards, and today this is a big challenge.
Another question is: will the development of entrepreneurship in the country be strengthened? That is one of the challenges which the provinces face today, and which I face in my ministry of small business. That commodity was once grown in abundance in the farming communities of Canada where people learned the value of adding to things, the value of trading something, and the value of needing a better way of doing something. Much of the innovation in our country came from these farm blacksmith shops, but as the population moved out of the farming communities into the urban centres, that natural crop of entrepreneurial ability was just not plentiful enough.
So today one of the challenges we have are the small business seminars. We find the Federal Business Development Bank needing CASE, this council advisory service that is so important in the community today. We find colleges now talking about entrepreneurial schools. All of this is part of urban life and constitutes an effort to replace that natural product which used to come from our farms.
Another question is: how can we maintain a balance of social programs so that we will help individual Canadians in need, while at the same time maintaining a strong work ethic and an incentive to work? I see that as I raise this subject my colleague, the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), rises to leave.

I am just changing chairs, sir.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Small Businesses and Industry
speechtext:
Well I am glad to see you resting again. Here is what has happened as we try to provide for all. This country has gone through two decades of wealth distribution and it has now come to the point where we find that we are not creating enough wealth to sustain the programs which we put in place. We were told years ago that a demand economy would be inflationary. The friend of the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Trudeau) warned us that the continuation of the demand economy would be inflationary. And what are we facing today? Public enemy No. 1 is inflation. If we continue with a demand type of economy, we will not address the problems of inflation, and that is one of the reasons why we have needed high interest rates today, rather than a retrenchment of supply of credit.
If we discipline ourselves, have some staying power, and eat beans for probably six months, we will find these interest rates coming down.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Beans?

speakerposition: Minister of State for Small Businesses and Industry
speechtext:
Sure, I am an optimist.
Another question is: how shall we keep the cost of social programs in government in total from becoming such a large burden to business in general and small business in particular? I have been addressing this question. The cost of government is just too great for business. It is a case of wealth creation will support wealth distribution, but I remind hon. members that today we are borrowing $1 billion a month to pay the bills. That is not wealth creation, that is just sucking the strength out of the nation. That is the challenge which this government must face, and that is the challenge with which it was left. The answers to this problem are not easy, and high interest rates is a tough answer for us to take right now.
Another question is: will we be able to produce settlements in the collective bargaining process which will avoid our country pricing itself out of international markets? I think that each segment of our community should address itself to this problem. We do need leadership in this area. There is no way that we can protect or sustain jobs if there is featherbedding underneath. If those jobs are working at a productivity level which allows us to generate wealth and take a truthful place in the domestic and global marketplace, then we can afford the programs which we have in place. If we fail to address some of those questions which I have put on the record tonight, we will miss the hour of challenge.

subtopic: SMALL LOANS ACT-AMENDMENTS TO PROTECT BORROWERS AGAINST HIGH INTEREST RATES
SMALL LOANS ACT-AMENDMENTS TO PROTECT BORROWERS AGAINST HIGH INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this has been a fascinating evening for me, to sit and listen to philosophical arguments both pro and con respecting the business community. The Minister of State for Small Businesses and Industry (Mr. Huntington) has expounded on what I believe to be the basic truth known to every homemaker in Canada, that if you do not have enough money when you go into the supermarket, you do not come out with enough groceries.
I have listened attentively and watched the expressions on the faces of hon. members on the other side, whom, I guess, we could call the disciples of the magic poke, who feel you can put your hand in that magic poke and dispense cash right, left, and centre, and that some time in the middle of the night the magic tooth fairy will come along and replace it. I have never understood that philosophy.
I think that the minister is to be congratulated for a clear dissertation on how the economy works and how the nation's affairs turn. I hope that the minister is successful not only with this piece of legislation but with any legislation which will help overcome the staggering deficit that we have inherited, and get us back on the true trail of free enterprise.
It is on this subject that I wish to speak tonight. Another influence on the small business community is the Small Loans Act. The Small Loans Act is a responsibility which is shared by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Lawrence) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie). Since mandated to do so, the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has undertaken a policy review of all such legislation coming under federal jurisdiction. This, of course, includes the Small Loans Act, which has come under close scrutiny.
In the course of review, representations have been received from industry urging quick action by the government to alleviate the impossible conditions which the lending company and customer members alike must endure. In fact, 1 am not sure that endure is the correct word. In many cases it should more properly be described as, "cease to function due to the number of loans being turned down because of high cost and lack of funds".
We recognize that the Small Loans Act was not designed to help the business side of the equation directly but, rather, to help the borrower. However, considering that co-operative credit unions and caisses populaires are usually member owned and operated, if they cannot operate profitably or effectively because of the restrictions of the act, they not only suffer

November 26, 1979
Adjournment Debate
themselves but also cause their clients distress and financial loss, while not providing the public with the protection and service intended in the act. This may be a decidedly convoluted argument, Mr. Speaker, but is clear and factual, nevertheless.
The overriding feature of the Small Loans Act is the graduated limit it imposes on loans of value less than $1,500. The upper limit for such loans is about 15 per cent interest, on a graduated scale. The purpose of such a ceiling was to protect small borrowers, high risk borrowers in many cases, from higher interest rates than could be enjoyed by more regular borrowers. The act was brought in at a time when the chartered banks, for reasons of prestige or security, did not encourage or accept consumer loans of this type, and at a time when other available sources of funds were not as plentiful and as reputable as many institutions which make up the small loans industry today.
The chartered banks are exempt from the provisions of the act. Other lenders, however, such as trust companies, finance companies and, of course, the co-operative credit unions and caisses populaires, must operate under the restriction and handicap to which the chartered banks are not exposed. As a result, there is a great lessening of competition in the small loans market, and a substantial falling off in the number of loans sought and issued.
High interest rates have made it unprofitable for small loans companies to serve the small loan borrower, as the interest ceilings make it impossible for the lenders to recover the costs of lending transactions and bad debts which attend these kinds of high risk loans. Thus, while the companies are suffering, so too are the borrowers. Their request for small loans under $1,500 are being refused because there just are no sub 15 per cent funds available. The result in many cases, especially where loans of $1,200 or $1,300 are desired, is that borrowers are forced to borrow more than $1,500-more than they need or want, thus incurring an increased debt burden and still having to pay the higher than 15 per cent interest rate, the very thing from which the act was supposed to protect them.
If, on the other hand, the borrower decides to go to another lending institution, he must still pay the higher interest rates to such institutions which are not restricted by the act. An even more sinister scenario is where the borrower, being unable to qualify for a loan from institutions which do not cater to higher risk requests, is forced to resort to a loan shark, with all the ugly consequences that conjures up.
You can see, Mr. Speaker, that this is a "no win" situation. When well-intentioned government restriction interferes with the free market forces, everybody suffers. In this case, the company cannot lend, the consumer cannot borrow, the money is not cheaply available, the job does not get done, the bill cannot be paid, the recreation room is not built, the plumbing is not fixed, the economy is not stimulated, and the whole high cost recession cycle is boosted a little further on its way.
For all these reasons, the Small Loans Act is a classic example of government regulation which has outlived its use-

fulness and now harms the very element of society it was designed to protect. Any other benefits incorporated in the Small Loans Act, such as the right of the borrower to prepay loans before maturity, without penalty, or to provide an instrument for the prosecuting and penalizing of loan sharks, could and should be incorporated in the Bank Act and/or Criminal Code.
The urgency occasioned by the imported high interest rate problem of recent weeks has imposed an impossible burden on the member owned co-operatives, small loan companies, and caisses populaires. Speedy repeal of the Small Loans Act would provide the vitally needed relief which, I am certain, would be wished by ail members of this House for the benefit of the small loan borrower.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ron Ritchie (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: SMALL LOANS ACT-AMENDMENTS TO PROTECT BORROWERS AGAINST HIGH INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to be able to bring some assurance to the hon. member which I hope he will find encouraging.
As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) indicated in this chamber on November 14, he is well aware that the Small Loans Act is in need of revision and, in particular, that the interest rate ceilings in the act are inappropriate under today's conditions. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Lawrence), whose department has in recent years been charged with the responsibility for generating policy relating to consumer credit generally, is also aware of the problem. He shares the view that this is definitely an area that requires early action. Officials of his department and of the Department of Insurance, which has continued to carry out the day to day administration of the act under the direction of the Minister of Finance pending clarification of the status of the act as an element of consumer credit protection, have been actively discussing possible changes.
Legislative proposals relating to the matter will be brought forward as soon as reasonably possible. It may be determined that the act no longer serves a useful purpose in today's environment. As a minimum, it can be expected that the interest rate ceilings will be revised and that the position under the act of financial institutions such as credit unions and caisses populaires will be dealt with. There is good reason to believe that it was never intended that such financial institutions should be subject to all of the provisions of the act. When the act was last revised in 1956, credit unions and caisses populaires were not nearly as large as they are now. Moreover, until quite recently, they were limited by provincial law to a maximum interest rate of 1 per cent per month. Thus, at the last revision the act was designed primarily to deal with the activities of those financial intermediaries that were then active in the field.
A somewhat anomalous situation, as just described by the hon. member, has arisen as a result of the general upturn in interest rates in recent years, since money lenders such as credit unions and caisses populaires must now obtain licensed status under the act if they wish to charge rates greater than 1

per cent per month. The licensing of thousands of such lenders and inspection of their affairs present an enormous administrative workload for the Department of Insurance. Nevertheless, licensing is available and the department is prepared to use its best efforts in processing any such requests as quickly as possible. This would provide interim relief for such institutions pending adoption of the legislative proposals to which I have alluded.

subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-REQUEST FAMILY ALLOWANCE PROGRAM RETAIN PRINCIPLE OF UNIVERSALITY
SOCIAL SECURITY-REQUEST FAMILY ALLOWANCE PROGRAM RETAIN PRINCIPLE OF UNIVERSALITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, following up on my question of November 5 concerning the government's intentions with regard to the universality of the family allowance program, I would like at this point to give several reasons why we believe it is so important to maintain universality, and then invite the parliamentary secretary's response to my arguments.
Universal programs such as those we now have in education, pensions, health care, and family support, that is, family allowances, are not just techniques for distributing benefits to individuals in our society. They are a statement about what kind of society we are. Universality states that, as a society, we put a high priority on some benefits such as education, health, support for our elders and family life, and that we are prepared to support these things out of the general wealth of the community because it is as important to the so-called poor that the so-called rich have their health, for example, as it is to the so-called rich that the so-called poor are looked after. This is a view which reinforces our view of Canadian society as a community and not just a collection of wealthy and needy individuals.
People should receive benefits simply because they are people, and because we belong to each other. Universal programs as such are not to be seen as welfare programs or as ways of redistributing wealth per se. This is why the government's apparent intention to de-universalize the family allowance program, or to do away with it altogether in order to make for more effective income redistribution, is such a serious, practical and conceptual error.
It is a dangerous conceptual error because it sets up all universal programs for the same criticism, although from another angle in other cases. For instance, in the case of universal education programs, these could be criticized for redistributing wealth upwards, as it is the children of the affluent who use the education system more than others. However, we still say that education should be universally available.
The fact that the gap between rich and poor has become even wider rather than narrower cannot be blamed on universal programs but, rather, on the fact that we still have not seen a fair tax system come into being in this country.
Adjournment Debate
Third, the government's apparent intention is a dangerous practical error, as in practice there would be very little likelihood that those who would supposedly benefit from these changes would see any net improvements in their general welfare. The open agenda of this government is to save money. Therefore, money received through increased child tax credits, for instance, is likely to be lost or reduced through eliminated family allowances or through some other re-shuffling of the same money. Money may simply be redistributed, for instance, from women to men, as many women depend on the family allowance program for their sole source of income.
There are those, I realize, who are hard-pressed to criticize the government's apparent move toward selectivity in social programs, as the argument about targeting money more effectively to those who need it most appeals to our charitable instincts, but this assumes that funds available for social programs have reached their limit and that the status quo is it. We in the New Democratic Party do not accept this argument.
It is the counsel of despair, and we advise the minister to count upon the good will, the generosity, and the sense of the common good which Canadians have in abundance, and seek ways of closing the gap between the rich and the poor, which actually increase government revenue in this vital area of programming, and not just play around with the limits of the budget given him by his colleagues at the Treasury Board. I challenge him-in this case the parliamentary secretary on his behalf-to commit the department to this end and to guarantee, should the government go ahead with this bad mistake, that at the very least all money saved on the one hand will be put back into social programs on the other, whatever they may be, and I do not mean expensive campaign promises.
